read.sections.0.heading.source: Schools are deciding how to use AI
read.sections.0.heading.back: Schools are deciding how to use AI

read.sections.0.text.source: AI chat tools can answer questions, explain ideas and even write whole essays. Many people use them, including many students. So schools and families face a new question: how should students use these tools? In 2023, UNESCO, the United Nations organisation for education, asked more than 450 schools and universities. Fewer than 1 in 10 had rules or formal guidance about AI tools. Later that year, UNESCO wrote guidance for countries. It said they should protect students' privacy, and set an age limit, such as 13, for children using these chat tools on their own. This is advice, not a law, and it is not about every learning tool.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI chat tools can answer questions, explain ideas, even write whole compositions. Many people use them, including many students. So schools and families face a new question: how should students use these tools? In 2023, UNESCO, the UN organisation for education, asked more than 450 schools and universities. Fewer than 1 in 10 had official rules or guidance about AI tools. Later the same year, UNESCO wrote guidance for countries. The guidance said countries should protect students' privacy, and set an age limit, for example 13, for children using these chat tools alone. This is advice, not a law, and not about every learning tool.

read.sections.1.heading.source: A tool can help you learn
read.sections.1.heading.back: A tool can help you learn

read.sections.1.text.source: Used well, an AI tool can work a bit like a tutor. It can explain a hard idea in simpler words, give you extra practice or translate a page into a language you know. At the made-up Brightwater School, Mira asks the homework helper to explain fractions in a new way. Then she does the practice herself. In 2024, researchers tested an AI tutor for English with secondary school students in Nigeria. For six weeks, students used it after school, and trained teachers guided every session. On English tests at the end, they did better than students who did not take part.
read.sections.1.text.back: If used well, an AI tool can be a little like a tutor. It can explain a hard idea in simpler words, give you extra practice, or translate a page into a language you know. At the made-up Brightwater School, Mira asks the homework helper tool to explain fractions in a new way. Then she does the practice herself. In 2024, researchers tested an AI tutor for English with secondary school students in Nigeria. For six weeks, the students used it after school, and teachers who had been trained guided every session. In English tests at the end, their results were better than students who did not take part.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: An AI tool can be a bit like a tutor. It can explain a hard idea in easy words, or give you more practice. At Brightwater School, Mira asks the helper about fractions. read.sections.1.simpler.back: An AI tool can be a little like a tutor. It can explain a hard idea in easy words, or give you extra practice. read.sections.2.heading.source: A tool can also be a shortcut
read.sections.2.heading.back: A tool can also become a shortcut

read.sections.2.text.source: An AI tool can also become a shortcut that gets in the way. In a study in Türkiye, nearly 1,000 high school students practised maths. Some used a chat tool that gave full answers. They did better in practice, but worse on a test without the tool. Students whose tool gave hints, written with teachers' help, did about as well as students with no tool. Each study was one subject in one place, so results elsewhere may differ. A tool can also be wrong and still sound sure, and not every student has a device. So Brightwater's draft rules ask for hints first, honest work and checks with a teacher.
read.sections.2.text.back: An AI tool can also become a shortcut that actually gets in the way. In a study in Türkiye, nearly 1,000 senior high school students practised maths. Some used a chat tool that gave full answers. Their practice results were better, but their test results without the tool were worse. Students whose tool gave hints, written with teachers' help, got about the same results as students with no tool. Each study was only about one subject in one place, so results in other places may differ. A tool can also be wrong but still sound sure, and not every student has a device. So Brightwater's draft rules ask for hints first, honest work, and checking with a teacher.
read.sections.2.text.note: "Türkiye" kept as the English text writes it, which Indonesian government usage now also follows; everyday Indonesian says "Turki". "High school" became "SMA".

read.sections.2.simpler.source: A tool can also be a shortcut. Then you learn less. In one study, nearly 1,000 students practised maths. Some had a tool that gave full answers. They did well in practice. On a test with no tool, they did worse. Others had a tool that gave hints, made with teachers. They did as well as students without one. Results may differ in other places. A tool can be wrong but sound sure. Not everyone has a device. Brightwater's rules say: hints first, honest work, and check with a teacher.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: A tool can also become a shortcut. As a result, you learn less. In one study, nearly 1,000 students practised maths. Some had a tool that gave full answers. Their practice results were good. In a test without the tool, their results were worse. Other students had a tool that gave hints, made with teachers. Their results were as good as students without a tool. Results in other places may differ. A tool can be wrong but sound sure. Not all students have a device. Brightwater's rules say: hints first, honest work, and check with a teacher.

watch.summary.source: This short cartoon is about AI chatbots. A chatbot is a computer program you can chat with in writing. It is a bit like sending messages to a person. The video explains what chatbots are and how they work. It also asks why many of them are made to sound like people. A chatbot can sound friendly and human. This can make it feel like a friend. It can also make its answers feel more true than they are. But a chatbot is not a person. It does not really know you, and it can be wrong. So notice how a chatbot makes you feel. And check what it says before you trust it.
watch.summary.back: This short cartoon is about AI chatbots. A chatbot is a computer program you can chat with in writing. It feels a little like sending messages to someone. The video explains what a chatbot is and how it works. It also asks why many chatbots are made to sound like humans. A chatbot can sound friendly and human-like. This can make it feel like a friend. It can also make its answers feel more true than they really are. But a chatbot is not a human. It doesn't really know you, and it can be wrong. So notice what you feel because of a chatbot. And check what it says before you trust it.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Don't ask learners whether or how they have used AI tools for schoolwork, and don't ask them to type questions into a real AI tool in class. UNESCO's 2023 guidance asks countries to set an age limit for children's independent conversations with generative AI tools (its press release names 13); it is guidance, not a rule for every learning tool, and many learners are younger. The pretend tool keeps everyone offline. UNESCO's wording differs between sources: its catalogue record says the guidance proposes "setting an age limit for independent conversations with GenAI platforms"; its press release says it "sets an age limit of 13 for the use of AI tools in the classroom". sensitiveNotes.0.back: Don't ask learners whether or how they have used AI tools for schoolwork, and don't ask them to type questions into a real AI tool in class. UNESCO's 2023 guidance asks countries to set an age limit for children's independent conversations with generative AI tools (its press release names 13); it is guidance, not a rule for every learning tool, and many learners are younger than that. educatorNotes.1.source: The two studies, simplified (see sources and claims/DW11.md). Nigeria: a World Bank randomised trial in public senior secondary schools in Edo State (Benin City), June to July 2024: six weeks of after-school English sessions, twice a week, with a large language model and teachers trained to guide each session; on a pen-and-paper test of English, AI knowledge and digital skills, gains were about 0.3 standard deviations (0.23 to 0.24 on English), and students also did better on end-of-year exams. The authors can't separate the AI from the teacher support and prompts, and don't know if it lasts or works in other subjects or ordinary classes. Türkiye: Bastani and others (PNAS, 2025): nearly 1,000 high school maths students; with GPT-4 during practice, the plain chat tool raised practice grades by 48% but lowered grades on a later exam without AI by 17%; the hint-giving tutor, with teacher input, raised practice grades by 127% and left exam grades about the same as no AI. Neither study shows an effect for every learner, subject or tool.
